passage:
Staff note, Monday.
After the flood, Vidya came to me before first period and asked if she could ride to the flooded colony alone with a bag of clothes. I explained that the water and roads were still unsafe and that the relief drive needed helpers right here. She went quiet and looked disappointed, then asked which jobs were open. By afternoon she was in the hall with four classmates, sorting clothes into piles, and she made a tally sheet for tins and blankets, updating it every time the van left. I checked on her twice and thanked her. She said she felt more useful with a list than she would have on a lonely road. The final list went to the ward office with the van driver.
— Preeti, class teacher

qa.q: What did Vidya make for the relief drive?
qa.a: She made a tally sheet for tins and blankets, updating it every time the van left.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when told she could not ride to the colony alone, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt disappointed, because she went quiet, but she soon became eager to help, since she asked which jobs were open.

qa.q: What could Vidya do if she wants more contact with the people affected, and why?
qa.a: She could ask her teacher whether the drive can arrange a visit with adults, because going alone would risk unsafe roads.

qa.q: How might families in the flooded colony benefit from Vidya's sorting?
qa.a: They may never meet her, but sorted blankets and tins reach them faster through the van and the ward office than one lone visitor could manage.

grounding: After a flood, a teen joins the school relief drive under a teacher's supervision, sorting donations and updating lists, instead of travelling alone to unsafe areas.

passage:
Wednesday
Day three of the school relief drive. Sachin wanted to take the bus to the flooded villages himself with a bag of biscuits. I almost went with him. Then Mrs Kulkarni said the roads there are still unsafe and the district team decides where things go, so we can do more good here.
So here's what I did today, 2 to 6 pm, in the school hall with Mrs Kulkarni watching over us: sorted three cartons of clothes by size, checked every food packet for its expiry date, and typed up the list of what came in, so the district team knows exactly what's on the truck. 146 items today.
Boring? A bit. But at 5:30 the truck left with everything labelled, and the driver said the camp can hand things out in minutes because of the lists.
Sachin did the lists with me in the end. He said it felt less heroic, but more useful.
– Vinita

qa.q: How many items went on today's list?
How did Vinita feel about the day's work?
qa.a: Vinita found it a bit boring, but satisfied and proud when the driver said the lists would help the camp.

qa.q: Why is working through the school drive better than travelling alone to the villages?
qa.a: The roads are unsafe and the district team knows where help is needed, so organised sorting reaches people faster and more safely.

qa.q: How does Sachin feel about ending up on the lists?
qa.a: Sachin felt it was less heroic than he'd hoped, but more useful.

grounding: Shows a teen joining a school relief drive under teacher supervision, sorting donations and updating lists instead of travelling alone to unsafe areas.

Anjali: some of us are taking scooties to the flooded side tomorrow to give food directly. coming?
Sahil: i asked Mr Joshi about that. he says the bridge there isn't cleared and they're asking people not to go
Anjali: but people need help NOW
Sahil: they do. the school's relief drive runs 3-7 in the gym, and the district team collects every evening
Sahil: yesterday i sorted hygiene kits and wrote the lists. they went out on the 7 pm truck
Anjali: sorting boxes feels useless tho
Sahil: honestly i thought so too. then Mr Joshi showed me the camp's message: they needed exactly what we'd listed
Anjali: ok... what do i do if i come
Sahil: bring your laptop. they need someone to update the donations sheet
Anjali: fine. 3 pm. and nobody takes scooties
Sahil: deal 👍

qa.q: When does the school's relief drive run?
qa.a: The drive runs 3-7 in the gym.

qa.q: Why does Anjali want to go to the flooded side herself?
qa.a: Anjali feels urgent and worried that people need help now, and sorting boxes seems useless.

qa.q: What makes Sahil's way of helping safer and still useful?
qa.a: It follows Mr Joshi's advice to avoid the uncleared bridge, and the district team takes the listed supplies where they're needed.

qa.q: How might the camp workers see the labelled lists?
qa.a: They receive exactly what they asked for, clearly listed, which makes handing things out faster.

grounding: Shows a teen joining a school relief drive under teacher supervision, sorting supplies and updating lists instead of travelling to unsafe flooded areas.
